comparison: Perfect agreement on claims C30-C31, C46, C50, C87. Both evaluations find the evidence for reduced connectivity during stimulation convincing and supported. Reviewers describe this as 'very interesting' and OpenEval notes strong statistical evidence (p<0.001) from mixed-effects models.

Perfect agreement on claims C32-C34, C44, C52, C63. Both evaluations support the finding that intrinsic dynamics enhance and prolong stimulus responses. Reviewers affirm 'recurrent brain activity enhances and prolongs the putative neural responses' and OpenEval cites strong statistical evidence (p<0.0001, p=0.0002).

Perfect agreement on claims C40-C42, C47, C51, C88. Both evaluations support the finding of reduced intrinsic noise during stimulation. Reviewers note this as a key finding and OpenEval provides strong statistical support (p=8.8×10⁻⁷), though notes the gain adaptation mechanism (C88) remains somewhat speculative.

Perfect agreement on claims C43, C48 with shared uncertainty. Both evaluations note the hierarchical connectivity finding but acknowledge the critical caveat in C85 that the correlation becomes non-significant when normalizing for electrode density, substantially undermining confidence in this result.

Perfect agreement on claims C81-C82, C91-C92. Both evaluations support the validation analysis using simulated data. Reviewers explicitly note validation on neural mass model data as a strength, and OpenEval reports consistent correlation values (0.69-0.70) while acknowledging limitation to simulated data.

Strong agreement on claims C35-C38, C62 (OpenEval also includes C63). Both evaluations support the parallel findings across LFP and BHA signal types. Reviewers note intracranial EEG as a strength, and OpenEval emphasizes consistency across signal types strengthens overall conclusions despite expected differences in sparsity.

Strong agreement on claims C23-C29 (peer review also includes C21-C22, C45). Both evaluations strongly support the finding that accounting for stimulus reduces spurious connectivity. Reviewers affirm this protects against misidentifying stimulus responses as connectivity, and OpenEval cites converging statistical evidence (p<0.0001) from 26 sessions.

Strong agreement on claims C17-C18, C75-C78 (OpenEval also includes C71-C72). Both evaluations support the VARX framework and its positioning relative to existing methods. Reviewers describe VARX as 'interesting' and 'original,' and OpenEval notes accurate technical comparisons with DCM and computational advantages.

Agreement on claims C53-C54 but with different emphasis. OpenEval rates as SUPPORTED, noting prior published work and appropriate acknowledgment of limitations. Peer review rates as UNCERTAIN, emphasizing the editor's note that 'one must specify all sensory features in the model, which is not possible,' qualifying conclusions about connectivity reduction.

Agreement on methodological claims C90, C96-C97, C100-C102 (OpenEval also includes C98-C99, C103-C104; peer review includes C89, C93-C95). Both evaluations support the methodological details as appropriate and sufficient. Reviewers note intracranial EEG and code availability as strengths.

Partial overlap on main conclusions C21-C22. OpenEval R6 focuses on how multiple lines of evidence support the main conclusions, while peer R1 focuses more specifically on the spurious connectivity finding (C23-C29, C45). Both are supportive but emphasize different aspects of the overall conclusion.

Partial overlap on background claims C2-C5, C10 (OpenEval includes C1, C6-C9, C11-C12; peer includes C72). Both evaluations support the characterization of the field and motivation for the study. Reviewers implicitly accept this by affirming the paper 'tackles an important issue,' and OpenEval notes appropriate citations to established literature.

Partial overlap on dataset description C89, C93-C95. OpenEval R10 focuses on dataset characteristics as internally consistent and substantial, while peer R11 focuses more broadly on methodological strengths including intracranial EEG and code availability. Both are supportive.

OpenEval evaluates parameter exploration claims C103-C104 as supported, noting empirical documentation of trade-offs and justified choice of na=6. No corresponding peer review evaluation found for these specific methodological details.

OpenEval evaluates fixation onset timing claims C83-C84 as supported, noting appropriate acknowledgment of complexity in treating fixation onsets as external inputs. No corresponding peer review evaluation found for these specific methodological caveats.

OpenEval evaluates the electrode density confound claims C85-C86 as supported, noting appropriate transparency about limitations. While peer R5 mentions this caveat, there is no separate peer evaluation specifically focused on these limitation claims.

OpenEval evaluates literature review claims C13-C16, C55, C57, C64-C65, C67-C69 as supported, noting accurate summaries with appropriate citations. No corresponding peer review evaluation found for these specific background literature claims.

OpenEval evaluates methodological context claims C19-C20, C60-C61, C70 as supported, noting appropriate justifications and physiological background. No corresponding peer review evaluation found for these specific contextual claims.

OpenEval evaluates theoretical interpretation claims C58-C59, C66 as UNCERTAIN, noting they are explicitly speculative and go beyond what data directly demonstrate, though consistent with theoretical frameworks. No corresponding peer review evaluation found for these specific theoretical claims.

OpenEval evaluates alternative approaches claims C73-C74 as supported, noting accurate descriptions with appropriate citations. No corresponding peer review evaluation found for these specific literature comparison claims.

OpenEval evaluates example observation claim C39 as supported, noting it is appropriately qualified as an example from one patient. No corresponding peer review evaluation found for this specific descriptive observation.
